system:
You repair one knowledge atom that auditors sent back. Use only the supplied evidence sentences; add no background knowledge.

Rules for the repaired atoms:
- One independently assessable claim per atom, written as one sentence that is understood without the source.
- If the atom joined several claims, split it into separate atoms (at most 3), most important first.
- Every atom must be fully stated in the evidence sentences it cites. Remove anything the evidence does not state. Keep quantifiers, negation, hedges, and formulas (LaTeX in $...$).
- Remove procedural or evaluative add-ons and stacked conditions; keep a condition only if the claim is false without it.
- Drop attributions such as "the authors state" when the claim itself is general.
- Use the S label that fits: S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends.
- If no valid atom can be written from this evidence, return an empty list and explain in note.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"atoms": [{"statement": "...", "scope": "S1|S2|S3", "evidence_ids": ["..."]}], "note": ""}
user:
CONCEPT: Asynchronous error handling

ATOM DPCPP2-C08-S3-01 (S3): Relying on error detection during program teardown does not work in all cases; for example, if a program terminates only when a convergence criterion is met that requires successful device kernel execution, an asynchronous exception may mean convergence never occurs and teardown, where the error would be noticed, is never reached.

EVIDENCE:
[DPCPP2-p0178-s07] Relying on error detection during program teardown doesn’t work
[DPCPP2-p0178-s08] in all cases, though. For example, if a program will only terminate when some algorithm convergence criteria are achieved and if those criteria are only achievable by successful execution of device kernels, then an asynchronous exception may signal that the algorithm will never converge and begin the teardown (where the error would be noticed).

AUDITOR FINDINGS:
- L1_ONLY: revise — Remove the convergence example with stacked conditions; retain the limitation that teardown-based detection is not always sufficient. / Carries a multi-condition hypothetical example ('if a program terminates only when... and...'). Keep only the core fact that teardown detection fails if an error prevents reaching teardown.
